# Overview

Studies 1 and 2 showed that the share of high-surprisal tokens tracks
proficiency. Study 3 asks what those tokens are. A token is *high* when its
surprisal under the Study 1 configuration (OLMo-2 1B, 8-token window) exceeds
τ, the 90th percentile of token surprisal in the strongest third of ELLIPSE dev
essays.

Two corpora are used.

- **W&I+LOCNESS** (BEA-2019; Yannakoudakis et al. 2018) has expert corrections.
  It holds learner essays at CEFR levels A, B and C and 50 essays by native
  student writers (LOCNESS, level N). Every high token is either corrected by
  the annotator (an error) or left alone (acceptable). This answers *how much*
  of the surprisal is error, with no model involved.
- **ELLIPSE** is the corpus of Studies 1 and 2. It has no corrections, so it is
  where the LM repairs are applied as essay profiles against the human scores.

The LM repair method asks the same model which minimal edit would make the text
expected, which names *what kind* of error a token is. It is checked against
the W&I corrections before it is read on ELLIPSE. The proposal's δ-vector
method, and why it does not answer the question, is in `appendix/appendix.qmd`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(knitr)
source("src/1-predictability-benchmark/_viz_helpers.R")
R3 <- "results/study3"
TH <- fromJSON(file.path(R3, "threshold.json"))
LEVELS <- c("A", "B", "C", "N")
gt <- fromJSON(file.path(R3, "gold_tests.json"))
lv <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "gold_by_level.csv")) |> mutate(level = factor(level, LEVELS))
fmt_rho <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", x$rho, x$ci[1], x$ci[2])
```

τ = `r sprintf("%.2f", TH$tau_bits)` bits, which means the model gave the
observed word a probability below about 1 in 2,500. It is fixed on ELLIPSE dev
and applied unchanged to every corpus.

# 1. How much of high surprisal is error

```{r}
#| label: threshold
thr <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "gold_threshold.csv")) |> mutate(level = factor(level, LEVELS)) |> arrange(level)
thr |>
  transmute(level, `tokens` = n_tokens, `above τ` = n_high,
            `corrected token` = share_of_high_ERR_TOK, `word missing before it` = share_of_high_ERR_INS,
            `follows an error` = share_of_high_POST, `left uncorrected` = share_of_high_OK) |>
  kable(digits = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "W&I+LOCNESS: what the annotator did with the tokens above τ, as shares of those tokens")
```

A token counts as an error when the annotator changed it, or inserted a word
just before it (an omission surfaces at the next word). Tokens right after a
corrected token are kept apart, since they may owe their surprisal to the error
before them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-decomposition
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
dec <- lv |>
  select(level, Errors = err_rate, Acceptable = acc_rate, `Follows an error` = post_rate) |>
  pivot_longer(-level, names_to = "part", values_to = "per_1000") |>
  mutate(part = factor(part, c("Errors", "Follows an error", "Acceptable")))
p <- ggplot(dec, aes(level, per_1000, fill = part)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Errors = "#b2182b", `Follows an error` = "#ef8a62", Acceptable = "#2166ac"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Level (N = native writers)", y = "High-surprisal tokens per 1,000") +
  theme_study1()
save_fig(p, "gold_decomposition", 7, 3.5, dir = R3)
p
```

```{r}
#| label: rates
lv |>
  transmute(level, essays = n_essays, `all above τ` = high_rate, errors = err_rate, acceptable = acc_rate,
            `follows an error` = post_rate, `acceptable share` = acc_share) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Mean rate per 1,000 tokens by level. Acceptable share is acceptable / (acceptable + errors)")
tibble(rate = c("all above τ", "errors", "acceptable", "acceptable share"),
       key = c("high_rate", "err_rate", "acc_rate", "acc_share")) |>
  mutate(`ρ with level, learners (A < B < C)` = map_chr(key, ~ fmt_rho(gt$rho_with_level[[.x]])),
         `native − C, per 1,000` = map_chr(key, ~ {
           d <- gt$native_minus_C[[.x]]; k <- if (.x == "acc_share") 1 else 1000
           sprintf("%.1f [%.1f, %.1f]", k * d$diff, k * d$ci[1], k * d$ci[2])
         })) |>
  select(-key) |>
  kable(caption = "Essay-level Spearman ρ with CEFR level, and the native − C difference (95% bootstrap CIs over essays). The acceptable-share row is a proportion, not a rate")
```

High surprisal is two signals that move in opposite directions.

- **Errors fall steeply with proficiency**, from about
  `r round(lv$err_rate[lv$level == "A"])` per 1,000 tokens at A to
  `r round(lv$err_rate[lv$level == "C"])` at C.
- **Acceptable surprise rises**, from `r round(lv$acc_rate[lv$level == "A"])`
  to `r round(lv$acc_rate[lv$level == "C"])` per 1,000.
- **Total surprise still falls**, because errors fall faster than acceptable
  surprise rises. The total therefore understates how strongly errors track
  level (ρ = `r sprintf("%.2f", gt$rho_with_level$err_rate$rho)` for errors
  against `r sprintf("%.2f", gt$rho_with_level$high_rate$rho)` for the total).
- **Native writers are more surprising than C learners, not less.** Their
  error rate is at the C level, and the difference is acceptable surprise.

So the measure does not penalize unexpected but acceptable writing. The penalty
comes from errors. Whether acceptable surprise is *effective* writing is beyond
what the corrections can show, since they mark errors and not quality.

# 2. What acceptable surprise looks like

Each high token is looked up in the Dolma reference corpora built for Study 2.
A word counts as *attested* in context when both of its bigrams (with the
previous word and with the next word) occur in edited Dolma prose, and as *rare*
when it occurs fewer than once per million words there.

```{r}
#| label: types
ty <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "gold_types.csv"))
ty |>
  transmute(type = ttype, n, `share acceptable` = share_ok, A = share_ok_A, B = share_ok_B, C = share_ok_C,
            N = share_ok_N, `share of all errors` = share_of_errors) |>
  arrange(desc(`share acceptable`)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "W&I+LOCNESS tokens above τ by type: share left uncorrected, overall and by level (tokens that follow an error excluded)")
```

```{r}
#| label: rare-attested
ra <- gt$rho_with_level$rare_attested_acc_rate
```

- **Attestation separates acceptable from erroneous content words.** Rare words
  attested on both sides are the most reliably acceptable type of high token,
  and rare words in unattested combinations are close to a coin flip.
- **Nonwords, function words and punctuation lean towards error.** Proper nouns
  and numbers lean towards acceptable.
- **Rare, attested, acceptable words rise with proficiency**, from
  `r sprintf("%.1f", lv$rare_attested_acc_rate[lv$level == "A"])` per 1,000
  tokens at A to `r sprintf("%.1f", lv$rare_attested_acc_rate[lv$level == "C"])`
  at C and `r sprintf("%.1f", lv$rare_attested_acc_rate[lv$level == "N"])` for
  native writers (ρ with level `r fmt_rho(ra)`). They are a small part of
  acceptable surprise, most of which is common words in attested combinations.
- **Every type is more often acceptable from A to C.** The same kind of word is
  more likely to be used correctly by a stronger writer, so type alone is a
  weak guide to whether a given token is an error.

# 3. What the error is: LM repairs

For each high token, about 23 minimal single-word edits are proposed:

- another inflection of the word;
- a near spelling (edit distance 1 or 2);
- one of the model's top predictions in its place;
- deleting it;
- inserting one of the model's top predictions before it.

Each edit is scored by how much it raises the log-probability of the word and
the next five subwords, under the same model and window as the surprisal. An
edit has to pay for itself at 1 bit per character changed, a cost fixed in
advance from Shannon's estimate for English. The token's label is the best
paying edit, subclassed by what it changes (for example `INS_DET` for an
inserted determiner, `MORPH_S_V` for verb agreement, `FORM_NONWORD` for a
misspelling), or NONE when no edit pays. This adapts LM-based error correction
(Bryant & Briscoe 2018; Yasunaga et al. 2021) to explain the measure's own
surprisal.

Labels fall into three groups. *Grammatical* labels fix an inflection or a
spelling, or insert, delete or replace a function word or punctuation.
*Lexical* labels replace, delete or insert a content word. NONE means no edit
paid.

```{r}
#| label: repair-groups
rep <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "gold_repair.csv"))
rep |>
  filter(level_of == "group") |>
  transmute(group = label, n, `share corrected` = 1 - share_ok, `share of all errors` = share_of_errors,
            A = 1 - share_ok_A, B = 1 - share_ok_B, C = 1 - share_ok_C, N = 1 - share_ok_N) |>
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "W&I+LOCNESS: share of tokens in each repair group that the annotator corrected, overall and by level")
```

```{r}
#| label: repair-labels
rep |>
  filter(level_of == "label", n >= 200) |>
  transmute(label, n, `share corrected` = 1 - share_ok, `share of all errors` = share_of_errors) |>
  arrange(desc(`share corrected`)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "Share corrected by repair label (labels with at least 200 tokens)")
```

- **Grammatical labels lean towards error.** The group is corrected
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - rep$share_ok[rep$level_of == "group" & rep$label == "grammatical"]))`
  of the time, against `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * gt$base_share_corrected)` for
  all high tokens. Inserting a missing preposition or determiner, fixing a
  nonword, and fixing an irregular form or verb agreement are corrected 80–90%
  of the time. Swapping in a different function word is closer to even.
- **Lexical labels do not.** "The model expected a different content word" is
  as often an acceptable choice as an error, which is why a paying repair alone
  cannot decide whether a token is an error.
- **NONE is mostly acceptable**, but it still holds a fifth of all errors.
  These are errors with no single-word fix, such as word order or phrasing.
- **The same label is more often an error at lower levels**, from A to C, as
  with the token types.

Examples of winning edits on ELLIPSE (the full set is in
`results/study3/repair_cards.md`):

- nonword spelling: *atitude → attitude*, *thier → their*;
- real-word confusion: *thing → think*, *Specially → especially*;
- inflection: *described → describes*, *a street that look → looks*,
  *I have choose → chosen*;
- omission: *have [a] sort of*, *as [a] result*, *never too late [to] fix*.

# 4. Repairs as essay profiles (ELLIPSE)

Per essay, the rate of each label per scored token.

```{r}
#| label: profiles
pr <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "profiles_rho.csv"))
pr |>
  filter(str_starts(label, "group_")) |>
  transmute(group = str_remove(label, "group_"), `share of high tokens` = share_of_high,
            `ρ with Overall` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", rho_overall, lo, hi),
            `low` = per_1000_low, `mid` = per_1000_mid, `high` = per_1000_high) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "ELLIPSE (all 6,482 essays): rate per 1,000 tokens by Overall band (below 3, 3, 3.5 and above) and Spearman ρ with Overall (95% bootstrap CI)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-profiles
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
pp <- pr |>
  filter(!str_starts(label, "group_"), share_of_high >= .005) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(str_ends(label, "_CONTENT"), "lexical", "grammatical")) |>
  ggplot(aes(rho_overall, fct_reorder(label, rho_overall), colour = group)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), size = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(grammatical = "#b2182b", lexical = "#ef8a62"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Spearman ρ of the label's rate with Overall", y = NULL) +
  theme_study1(10)
save_fig(pp, "profiles_rho", 7, 5, dir = R3)
pp
```

- **Every frequent label except inserted punctuation is rarer in stronger
  essays.** The grammatical group falls most steeply, and the lexical group
  nearly as steeply.
- **The rate of high tokens with no paying repair rises slightly with
  Overall.** This matches the W&I result that NONE is mostly acceptable
  surprise.
- **The W&I levels show the same pattern** (`profiles_wi_levels.csv`). Almost
  every grammatical label falls from A to C, and native writers sit near the C
  level, with somewhat more spelling labels.

# Summary for the write-up

- **High surprisal is two opposite signals.** On W&I+LOCNESS, errors fall
  steeply with proficiency and acceptable surprise rises, so total surprise
  understates the error signal. Native writers have the most acceptable
  surprise, at a C-level error rate.
- **Attestation characterizes acceptable surprise.** Rare words in combinations
  attested in edited prose are the most reliably acceptable kind of high token,
  and their rate rises with level.
- **LM repairs name the error.** Grammatical repair labels lean towards
  corrected tokens, and the insertion, inflection and nonword labels are
  corrected 80–90% of the time. Content-word substitutions and NONE are mostly
  acceptable.
- **On ELLIPSE, repair profiles behave as error measures should.** Every
  frequent label but inserted punctuation falls with Overall, and unrepaired
  high tokens rise slightly.
